**Chapter 1** 

**The Phenomenon** 

An interest in property tax liens has never been more relevant or more exciting. The property tax lien phenomenon was not born out of the real estate transaction error that caused the foreclosure crisis of 2010; it was born out of taxpayers defaulting on the ad valorem tax. The phenomenon was aptly dubbed “the Other Crisis.” It is a nightmare for those who are losing but a dream maker for others who are gaining an increase in revenue. Taxing authorities hold a superior lien against all taxable property to enforce the payment of taxes. Tax sales finance local, city, and state government services, such as fire, police, 911, 411, 211, infrastructure, school districts, and libraries. When cash shortfalls occur because of unpaid property taxes, a sale has to take place. Delinquent property taxes result in extraordinary problems for local governments, which must provide critical services to their constituents. 

As you can see, the “subprime bubble” that caused a major crisis in the United States and other countries is not the same as property taxes going unpaid. When a mortgage note goes into a planned default, there may be insurance or federal government intervention for corporations and banks. When property taxes go unpaid, many local governmental services and jobs become hard to maintain. Foreclosure by recharacterization is a slippery slope. Many have challenged inconsistencies, and banks are unable to prove “true sale.” A “quiet title action” that addresses whether there was a sale for receivables between buyer and seller or a pledge of collateral for a loan could possibly prove to be a great defense. This is not so with property tax liens. Although the investment has a right-to-foreclose-after-redemption component, the object is to make interest on the investment. If it comes to foreclosure, you will not have the same issues the banks are having. This may be because of deceptive practices in lending that took place at the outset.

**Chapter 2** 

What Is a Tax Lien Certificate? What is a tax lien?   
I guess the best way to start is to first explain what a tax lien certificate is so we don’t get ahead of ourselves in the information without first defining the investment itself. Tax lien certificates are liens placed on property for nonpayment of property taxes. A tax lien sale is a public auction, maintained by state statute, of tax liens. They are sold for the amount of delinquent taxes, interest charges, and other related fees due to the county. This investment will not transfer ownership to property. It entitles a purchaser to full payment by a delinquent taxpayer of the full lien amount paid at the time of auction plus interest. This represents a secured loan to the taxpayer without knowledge of his or her ability to repay; the high redemption doesn’t always come because of the taxpayer but the lenders. The lenders do not want to lose their interest in the property, so most will redeem for the borrower. The percentage interest changes from state to state. I get into this later along with the fact that some states are lien states and some are deed states. If the taxes remain delinquent past what is called a “period of redemption,” a purchaser has a first-in-time right to foreclose on the lien to attain ownership of a property. This is a third-party lien so the rules are different than with a bank’s foreclosure rights. A third party must wait until the redemption period has passed to pursue foreclosure. Some investors look for the opportunity to foreclose on a lien while other investors look to make money on the interest collected with the lien, which the owner must pay at the time of redemption along with the face value of the lien. In many states, they also have what is known as end-of-the-year penalties, which means more money in your pocket if you continue to buy the subsequent liens. This is also explained later. 

When are tax lien sales held?  
The tax lien sales are only held as needed. You must check your local listings, or you can even invest at online auctions. The rules change all the time, but bid4asset.com has been around for a while and seems to be in good standing, meaning I haven’t heard any complaints so far. Perform your due diligence and begin. There are no fees to register and no auction completion fees for buyers. A buyer premium is an optional fee sellers can add to the winning bid amount of an auction to cover costs associated with their auction. The buyer premium percentage is indicated on the auction listing and included in the total purchase price paid by the buyer to seller. The fee is usually 10 percent, but some other fees may apply if the seller mentions them. These points are made on the website, so make sure you thoroughly explore the information given. As for your search locally, you can start with making a phone call to the tax assessor’s office, which is sometimes called the tax claim bureau, tax collector, etc. Nevertheless, a simple phone call or visit will get you to the right information. 

What do I say once I am there at the tax collector’s office? 

These people are hard at work so please be courteous. Being respectful will help you get exactly what you need. Bring donuts to them the next day if they help you out. When you speak to someone, you can ask first, “When is the next tax sale?” if it’s a lien state. Like I explained before, some states auction off tax lien certificates to property, and some states auction off tax deeds. So you must know the answer to what type of auction is held in your state for delinquent property taxes. The only way to know is to ask the tax collector or try your luck with an Internet search. I prefer that you build relationships with the people in the tax collector’s office because it will do you a world of good in the future. There are a few more things you need to consider when you visit the tax collector’s office. First, you will need to develop a *professional* e-mail address. You have to do this because they like to e-mail information these days and you are not going to be taken seriously if you give them an e-mail address like sweetness@gmail.com. Ask how and when you should register for the sale. Find out how they would like to be paid. Find out what the tax ratio is. Ask the right questions, be professional, and be there first thing in the morning. 

Other questions to ask include: • Can I preregister for the sale?  
• Is this an accelerated sale that includes last year’s taxes? • Does this county have an end-of-the-year penalty if payments that year exceed \$10,000? 

• Do I have access to this list on your website? 

• How do I ask for the list of delinquent property taxes? 

• One of my teachers made this part extremely difficult, but I have learned that it’s quite simple. I was taught to ask to look up only the utility liens for the previous year to determine the amount of property taxes that are open for the current year’s first quarter. Now, they can definitely set these limits for you on the office computer so you can print the list out and start your due diligence. The list is often printed in the newspaper or on the county’s website, but either way, you are going to get the list. 

• Will the list change before the auction date? 

Absolutely. This list is never final, so the best thing to do is to perform your “ride-bys” and out-of-the-office due diligence a week or even a few days before the sale. This will allow you to know exactly what you’re bidding on and give you the confidence that the property will be in the sale. This also is where I take issue with the infomercial guys. They sell you a list that is free without the promise that it is the final list. This list always changes. Why? People want to pay the taxes before the auction date most of the time, and that’s fair game because they have a chance at redemption. If the homeowner pays before the sale, he or she can evade the interest and, most important of all, become current again.  
**Chapter 3** 

**Due Diligence** 

Here is the most important part of your investment. This is where you purge your list on paper and then in person on a case-by-case road plan. I love this part because it gives you the facts you need to determine whether your investment is a good one or a bad one. There isn’t any guessing after due diligence is performed. Some say it is all location, and that is wonderful and correct, but mathematical factors and developing a neighborhood rating system won’t hurt as you reach toward a more excellent and valued approach. Due diligence is an informational requirement for a potential acquirer. This can be seen as voluntary, but you must make it a standard of care when engaging the target asset. If you are building a tax lien fund with a solo tax lien trust and whole life policy, the standard of care must be implemented to ensure a constant degree of increase in cash value to leverage for greater acquisitions. Your risk diminishes when this fund is properly erected. See avfnow.org if you are interested in quantifying your growth potential with a tax lien trust fund. 

Where do I begin with due diligence? 

If you are following along with this road map, then you are already engaging degrees of due diligence, so if you have already begun executing the previous steps after you have gathered your list of properties and have done all that you can do online, you are already ahead of the game. I will give you more tools you can use for your online research to better equip you and strengthen your investment choices. Next, it is time to ride by the properties. Remember, this should be done after getting an updated list from the tax collector’s office again and approximately one week to three days before the sale, depending on the number of properties you are researching. Most people use a key map from the city that has street names, but I say invest in a good GPS that you can place multiple addresses in and then optimize your list so the device can go to the properties closest to your current location. These devices are available, and they cost around two hundred dollars. This will save you so much time and headache. When I  
started out, we used maps that opened up as big as the inside of the car with no corresponding addresses and no one to tell us what the best route was. Take pictures if you can so you can identify which house is which when you are bidding on the day of the sale. 

What happens to the properties that go unsold? 

When property is offered for sale and an amount is not received that is equal to or in excess of the minimum sale price, the county executive acquires a lien in the amount of the minimum sale price. This lien attaches on the day after the last date on which the property was offered for sale. When a county executive acquires a lien as described, the county auditor will issue a tax sale certificate to the county executive. When a county executive acquires a tax sale certificate, the county executive has the same rights as a purchaser. The county executive may offer the certificate for sale via public auction, make it available over-the-counter, or simply retain the certificate. 

Can you buy tax liens by mail? 

There are some states that have private auctions through the mail for tax deeds, but the answer is no. You or another trustee, if you have a trust, must attend the public auction to bid for properties in the tax lien sale. 

What is the equalization rate, and why is it important? 

You should want to know from the tax collector what the equalization ratio is because this represents the percentage of the total value given in the total assessment.  
**Chapter 4** 

**The Acquisition** 

What type of payment is required? 

Each county has its own set of payment terms. The terms are announced during the introduction to the auction, so pay close attention. Lien buyers must pay the amount of their bids in the way acceptable to the county and by the deadline given at the outset. In most cases, payments are made to the county by certified funds on the day of the sale. 

What is given to me as proof of purchase? 

Normally, the auctioneer gives extensive instructions at the beginning of the sale on the procedure. Once all the properties are sold or the auctioneer ends the sale, you will have to go to another room to complete the sale. There you will be asked for the money and the name in which you want the lien to go. If you have a trust, then this is where you would give the name of the trust; if you do not, then you would just provide the name you want the lien certificate recorded in. To be more direct, after the buyer pays the amount of the winning bid, the buyer will be issued a certificate of sale for each lien purchased. If the property is redeemed during the redemption period, the lien buyer must surrender the certificate of sale to the county auditor to receive the funds the buyer is owed as a result of the redemption plus interest and fees. Keep all of your certificates in a safe place. 

Will the sale be final? 

Yes. Once the auctioneer says, “Sold,” the lien on the property is awarded to the successful bidder, and this person either wins by interest rate or highest premium bid. The buyer is then required to pay for the lien. 

Will other liens continue to encumber the property after sale?  
Yes, if they exist. Unfortunately, this does not extinguish other outstanding liens, but your tax lien takes precedence.

**Chapter 6** 

**Solo Tax Lien Fund Methodology** 

When you are starting a career in tax lien investing, it is important to know the law as it involves tax liens in the state in which you are investing, the economic climate in that state, and how to do the math. After all, these investments aid the community you are investing in tremendously. You buy a lien for the amount of back taxes the owner owes, and when it redeems, you are the first to get paid, with an opportunity to make anywhere from 12 to 36 percent interest. This wonderful opportunity to learn how to yield such interest on top of any investment is better than treasury notes or bank CDs, which are both yielding less than 1.5 percent to date. With the proper structure, you can ensure yourself several degrees of latitude. Some \$426 billion in state and local tax on real estate is owed in the United States each year. More than twenty-five states allow these investments to be sold to third-party investors. According to the National Tax Lien Association, 99 percent of sold liens are redeemed by the property owners. With guarantees at this rate, the right formula can make you an ultra-high-net-worth earner. No matter the class structure or starting salary used to invest, the right blueprint will definitely put you in the winners’ circle. 

Don’t worry if you do not know enough about legal structures and trust funds. I am going to show you briefly how this applies to you. Sometimes, I take it for granted that most know about trust fund designs. A trust is a fiduciary relationship in which one party, known as a trustor or settlor, gives another party, the trustee, the right to hold title to property or assets for the benefit of a third party, the beneficiary. There are many types, and the one that will be discussed here will be a solo tax lien trust. In brief, this is a trust specifically for compounding wealth with tax lien certificates. The trustor hereby irrevocably assigns, transfers, and sets over to the trustee all the rights, powers, options, titles, claims, and benefits the trustor now has or hereafter may acquire in and to the property tax liens in the trust. The trustor acknowledges that the trustee (you) has the unlimited right to hold, manage, buy, sell, and receive the proceeds of any property and tax lien certificates transferred to the trust, and the trustor specifically authorizes  
and directs all parties who may deal with the trust to deal entirely and exclusively with the trustee and not the trustor after the date of transfer. **Risk Analysis** 

In any investment, a thorough risk analysis will help you to make improved decisions. If you are constructing a tax lien trust, then a SWOT analysis is necessary after you’ve gathered the information needed to build. Investopedia.com says that when using a SWOT analysis, be realistic about the strengths and weaknesses of your organization. Distinguish between where your organization or trust is today and where it could be in the future. Also remember to be specific by avoiding gray areas and always analyze in relation to the competition (i.e., are you better or worse than the competition?). Obviously, you will be better because most investors do not build a tax lien trust fund; they invest with a financial services company or buy in pieces. Finally, keep your SWOT analysis short and simple; avoid complexity and over analysis since much of the information is subjective. Thus, use it as a guide and not a prescription. When a trust is erected, the trustees’ main job should be to make sure that the trust does not accumulate negative asset value. A risk analysis applies in many respects, including qualitative and quantitative techniques to reduce uncertainty of the outcomes and associated costs, liabilities, or losses. This is why there is a “Due Diligence” chapter in this book, which will give you an idea of what the cause-and-effect determination can be. Due diligence will lower the risk, thus making the investment more attractive, especially if you are looking to create a secondary market as a reseller of tax liens. The following is a bulletin posted by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency, US Department of the Treasury. It provides their risk management expectations of tax lien certificates. This is written to CEOs of all national banks, federal branches and agencies, department and division heads, and all examining personnel—not individual third-party investors, such as you (see below): 

Description: Risk Management Expectations 

PURPOSE  
In recent years, banks have increased their holdings of tax lien certificates, in part, because of active marketing by third-party vendors moreover because of their comparatively higher yields in a low interest rate environment. This document describes the risk management practices that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) expects banks to exercise when buying tax lien certificates. 

BACKGROUND 

When a property tax bill becomes delinquent, the taxing authority places a tax lien on the property. In many states, the taxing authority is authorized to sell tax liens by issuing tax lien certificates. A tax lien certificate transfers to a third party the taxing authority’s right to collect delinquent property taxes and the right to foreclose on the property. A tax lien has a superior priority status that supersedes any existing nontax liens, including first mortgages. Tax lien certificates accrue interest and fees and often generate attractive returns for an investor. The laws governing the redemption and transfer of tax lien certificates vary among states and municipalities. 

Prior to 1996, the OCC concluded that the purchase of tax lien certificates was an unsafe and unsound banking practice primarily because the bank would be advancing funds solely on the value of collateral, rather than on the borrower’s ability to repay. In 1996 the OCC revised this position and asserted that under certain conditions national banks could acquire tax lien certificates. Under section 24(7), national banks have the right to “discount and negotiate...evidences of debt” and the OCC’s Interpretive Letter No. 725, dated March 22, 1996, concluded tax lien certificates were “evidences of debt.” However, because national banks are prohibited from purchasing a delinquent taxpayer’s property (12 USC 29), state or local law must confirm that a tax lien certificate represents a security interest in the  
property and not title to the property. Thus, if delinquent property taxes are defined as debt under state or local law, and the tax lien certificate represents an interest in the debt, a national bank may purchase a tax lien certificate. If applicable law of a jurisdiction does not contain these conditions, a national bank may not purchase the tax lien certificates. 

RISKS 

The OCC views conforming tax lien certificates as extensions of credit. By purchasing a tax lien certificate, a bank is financing a taxpayer’s delinquent taxes with a real estate-secured loan. Tax lien certificates contain credit, operational (transaction and compliance), liquidity, and reputation risks. 

As with all extensions of credit, tax lien certificates have credit risk, which is the risk that the obligation will not be repaid. Although the credit risk in a tax lien certificate is somewhat mitigated by its structure, a tax lien certificate is fundamentally an interest in a delinquent tax obligation. A delinquent obligation indicates a high level of credit risk. Due to the level of credit risk in tax lien certificates, banks that purchase them should have policies, procedures, and other risk management practices in place to control the risk. 

Tax lien certificates have operational risk because of the notification and filing requirements and the potential effect of subsequent tax liens. This risk escalates when a bank owns tax liens from multiple jurisdictions. In addition, because tax lien certificates are considered real estate-secured loans for assessing legal permissibility, banks must comply with the real estate lending standards of 12 CFR part 34\.  
Tax lien certificates increase liquidity risk because they tie up funds for an extended period without generating interim cash flows. The redemption period (the period during which the delinquent taxpayer can bring taxes current) for a tax lien certificate may be as long as five years. 

Finally, tax lien certificates expose a bank to reputation risk. Banks that purchase tax lien certificates may face reputation risk if they undertake significant numbers of foreclosures arising from tax lien certificate holdings. Reputation risk is higher if the foreclosed properties are concentrated geographically. In the worst case, the bank could be portrayed as engaged in predatory lending practices if it is advancing funds on the value of the collateral, without knowledge of the taxpayer’s ability to repay. 

RISK MANAGEMENT EXPECTATIONS 

The OCC expects banks that purchase tax lien certificates to implement a risk management program to control the inherent risks. Banks need board-approved policies, procedures, and controls to address the credit, operational, liquidity, and reputation risk factors described above. In addition, the OCC has identified four specific concerns that must be addressed in a tax lien certificate risk management program. 

1\. The OCC’s anti-predatory lending standards 1 and guidance 2 prohibit a bank from making any loan based predominantly on the foreclosure value of the property. Therefore, a bank’s decision to purchase tax lien certificates must be based on the likelihood that the real estate taxes will be paid, not on the value of the real property securing the instrument. Banks will need to conduct a repayment analysis for each transaction. Sole or heavy reliance on historic repayment statistics does not  
demonstrate the repayment capacity of an individual property owner. 

2\. Banks need to establish concentration limits for tax lien certificates. Limits should be established for the overall volume and by property type and geographic location. To establish such limits, a bank will need to identify the type of real property securing the tax lien certificate, e.g., single-family residential, multifamily residential, commercial property, vacant or occupied property, unimproved land, etc. 

3\. Banks should know the condition of the property and whether there are factors that will increase or decrease its value, in particular whether there are any environmental issues. 

Because the OCC considers tax lien certificates to be the equivalent of real estate–secured loans, banks must comply with 12 CFR part 34, “Real Estate Lending and Appraisals.” When a bank has a real estate secured loan, either an appraisal or an evaluation is required, depending on the amount of exposure. Tax assessment valuations do not meet the standards detailed under 12 CFR part 34\. 

RISK RATING, ACCOUNTING, and RISK-BASED CAPITAL CONSIDERATIONS 

Tax lien certificates are considered extensions of credit and, as such, need to be assigned ratings in conformance with the bank’s risk rating system. Tax lien certificates with an interest in a personal residence should be analyzed like residential real estate mortgage loans; tax lien certificates with an interest in commercial property should be analyzed like commercial real estate loans. Because tax lien certificates arise through nonpayment of taxes, the repayment source has well-defined weaknesses, and a “substandard” classification is generally warranted.  
Although considered loans for purposes of assessing legal permissibility and risk management practices, banks should report tax lien certificates as “Other Assets” in the Reports of Condition and Income (call report). This is because tax lien certificates do not meet the definition of a loan contained in the call report instructions, which is, “...an extension of credit resulting from direct negotiations between a lender and a borrower. The reporting bank may originate a loan...or it may purchase a loan or a portion of a loan originated by another lender that directly negotiated with a borrower.” Because a tax lien certificate represents an interest in a tax obligation that resulted from no direct negotiations between the holder of the certificate and the property owner, or between the taxing authority and the property owner, a tax lien certificate does not meet the call report definition of a loan. 

Accrual status should be determined in accordance with call report instructions and the bank’s nonaccrual policy. Delinquency should be calculated from the date the taxes were due to the taxing authority. At the time an institution purchases a tax lien certificate, the property owner’s real estate tax payment obligation typically meets the criteria for nonaccrual status set forth in the call report instructions, and therefore, income should be recognized on a cash basis. As a consequence, tax lien certificates should be reported in the past due and nonaccrual schedule of the call report in the item for “Other Assets.” When income is recognized on a tax lien certificate, it should be reported as “Other Noninterest Income” in the call report. 

For risk-based capital purposes, tax lien certificates are not claims on the taxing authority and carry a 100 percent risk weight. 

Questions regarding this bulletin should be directed to the Credit Risk Policy Division at (202) 649-6670. 

Barbara Grunkemeyer  
Deputy Comptroller for Credit Risk Policy 

I placed this analysis in this book to show you that a credible source determines that the investments of tax lien certificates are considered extensions of credit and equivalent to real-estate-secured loans. They are a lucrative investment that banks and hedge fund executives will have on their balance sheets, so why not yours? It may be listed under “Other Investments,” but nonetheless, major institutions are chasing yield in this business. The risk analysis from the OCC shows reputation risks for major institutions because of the inherent nature of the investment, as it may lead to foreclosure. As a private tax-lien fund manager or trustee, you will be able to use the accrued interest to build a fund that becomes cash, a tax deferred compensation arrangement, and an interminable banking system.  
Glossary 

**accelerated sale**. When the current year’s taxes and/or other municipal charges remain owing and due after the statutory due date, the municipality may enforce the collection of those charges by offering for sale the property, which will cause a tax lien certificate to be sold and filed against the property and will become subject to foreclosure proceedings if not redeemed in a timely manner. 

**accrued interest**. A term used to describe an accrual accounting method when interest that is either payable or receivable has been recognized but not yet paid or received. Accrued interest occurs as a result of the difference in timing of cash flows and the measurement of these cash flows. 

**ad valorem tax**. A tax based on the assessed value of real estate or personal property. Ad valorem taxes can be property tax or even duty on imported items. Property ad valorem taxes are the major source of revenue for state and municipal governments. 

**assessor**. A local government official who determines the value of a property for local real estate taxation purposes. Assessors are trained to determine the fair market value of property. The figures that they derive will be used to calculate future property taxes. The assessor estimates the value of real property within a city’s, town’s, or village’s boundaries. This value is converted into an assessment, which is one component in the computation of real property tax bills. 

**asset**. Something of value. 

**assignee**. A person, company, or entity that receives the transfer of property, title, or rights from a contract. The assignee receives the transfer from the assignor. For example, an assignee may receive the title to a piece of real estate from an assignor.  
**assignor**. A person, company, or entity that transfers rights he, she, or they hold to another entity. The assignor transfers to the assignee. For example, a party (the assignor) that enters into a contract to sell a piece of property can assign the proceeds or benefits of the contract to a third party (the assignee). 

**auction**. Public sales in which goods or property are sold to the highest bidder. 

**beneficiary**. Anyone who gains an advantage and/or profits from something. In the financial world, a beneficiary typically refers to someone who is eligible to receive distributions from a trust, will, or life insurance policy. Beneficiaries are either named specifically in these documents or they have met the stipulations that make them eligible for whatever distribution is specified. 

**bid**. An offer made by an investor, a trader, or a dealer to buy a security. The bid will stipulate both the price at which the buyer is willing to purchase the security and the quantity to be purchased. 

**bid-rigging**. A scheme in which businesses collude so that a competing business can secure a contract for goods or services at a predetermined price. Bid-rigging stifles free-market competition, as the rigged price will be unfairly high. The Sherman Act of 1890 makes bid-rigging illegal under US antitrust law. Bid-rigging is a felony punishable by fines, imprisonment, or both. Sometimes this happens in tax lien auctions, but it is easily detected, so have nothing to do with it. 

**board of equalization**. A government entity whose purpose is to ensure uniform property tax assessments. 

**capital**. Financial assets or the financial value of assets, such as cash. 

**declaration of trust**. A written statement by a trustee to acknowledge that the property is held for the benefit of another. 

**default**. The failure to promptly pay interest or principal when due. Default occurs when a debtor is unable to meet the legal obligation of debt repayment.  
**delinquent**. The failure to accomplish what law or duty, such as the failure to make a required payment or to perform a certain action, requires. 

**disclosure**. The act of releasing all relevant information pertaining to a property that may influence an investment decision. 

**due diligence**. An investigation or audit of a potential investment. Due diligence serves to confirm all material facts in regards to a sale. 

**equalization rate**. A ratio of total assessed value for properties in a community to those properties’ true market values. This number represents the state’s or locality’s judgment of how closely assessed values match the market value. For example, an equalization rate of 90 percent would mean that, on average, the property in a community is being assessed at 90 percent of its market value. There would be no need for equalization if all municipalities assessed all property at *100 percent* of market value every year. 

**fiduciary**. A person legally appointed and authorized to hold assets in trust for another person. The fiduciary manages the assets for the benefit of the other person rather than for his or her own profit. 

**foreclosure**. The process of taking possession of a property as a result of a failure to keep up payments on an obligation. The process of enforcing a lien against property for nonpayment of delinquent taxes. Taxing authorities hold superior lien against all taxable property to enforce the payment of their taxes. 

**legal description**. Legally acceptable identification of real estate by one of the following: 

• the government’s rectangular survey 

• metes and bounds 

• recorded plat (lot and block) 

**leverage**. The use of various financial instruments or borrowed capital, such as margin, to increase the potential return of an investment. 

**levy**. The legal seizure of property to satisfy a debt.  
**lien**. A charge against property making it a security for the payment of a debt, judgment, mortgage, or taxes; it is a type of encumbrance. 

**millage rate**. A tax rate applied to property. Each mill represents one dollar of tax assessment per one thousand of assessed property value. 

**penalty**. If a tax lien certificate is not redeemed and exceeds ten thousand dollars, select states add an end-of-the-year penalty. 

**premium**. This is an amount over and above the tax lien certificate amount usually going upward in increments of one hundred dollars that the investor will pay to the municipality to acquire the lien. When premium is paid for a lien, it is not the lowest interest rate bid that wins the lien, but rather the highest premium. Premium is not bid in all states that sell liens. In some states, the interest rate is bid down, and the lien is sold to the investor who bids the lowest percent interest. In other states, the interest rate is kept constant while premium is bid for the lien, thus lowering your return on the lien (since in most states no interest is paid on premium). 

**property tax**. A tax assessed on real estate by the local government. The tax is usually based on the value of the property (including the land) you own. 

**real estate**. Land plus anything permanently fixed to it, including buildings, sheds, and other items attached to the structure. Although the media often refers to the “real estate market” from the perspective of residential living, real estate can be grouped into three broad categories based on its use: residential, commercial, and industrial. Examples of real estate include undeveloped land, houses, condominiums, townhomes, office buildings, retail store buildings, and factories. 

**real property**. The rights to use real estate. Real property includes but is not limited to: 

• personal residence owned in fee simple 

• a life estate to a farm 

• rights to use land under a lease 

• easements and other partial interest  
**redemption period**. A redemption period is the legal right of any borrower in foreclosure or tax default to pay off the total debt. This period is not the same in every state. 

**subsequent tax paying**. The act of paying next quarter taxes on an unredeemed certificate. Some states mandate this payment on lien holders, and some states pay top interest allowed by that state. 

**tax collector**. A person who collects unpaid taxes. 

**tax lien**. A debt attached against property for failing to pay taxes. A tax lien may be imposed for failing to pay the following taxes: 

• city 

• county 

• estate 

• income 

• payroll 

• sales 

• school 

**tax lien sale**. A tax lien sale is the sale, conducted by a governmental agency, of tax liens for delinquent taxes on real estate. It is one of two methodologies used by governmental agencies to collect delinquent taxes owed on real estate, the other being the tax deed sale. 

**third-party lien holder**. An investor other than a bank or mortgagor. 

**yield**. The income return on an investment. This refers to the interest or dividends received from a security and are usually expressed annually as a percentage based on the investment’s cost, its current market value, or its face value.
